name: 0.brief

input.task: Write the two briefs for issue. builder: the steps to make one pull request that meets every line of issue.expect. verifier: for each expect line, in the same order, what to run at the PR head (tests, the program, a script) and what result means PASS and what means FAIL; checks that only read the diff are not enough. If why is set, an earlier attempt failed for that reason, and both briefs must change course to avoid it.

issue.title: csv2json: add a --tsv flag to read tab-separated input
issue.problem: bin/csv2json.js reads stdin and always calls parse(text) with no separator, and it ignores every command-line argument. The CLI therefore always splits on commas. Tab-separated input comes out as one column whose key is the whole header line, for example `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints [{"a\tb":"1\t2"}]. src/parse.js already accepts a separator as its second argument (sep = ','), but nothing in the CLI exposes it. The README documents only CSV usage.
issue.reason: The user's exports now arrive as TSV, so before every run they have to convert tabs to commas with sed. That extra step also corrupts any field that contains a literal comma.
issue.outcome: `node bin/csv2json.js --tsv < table.tsv` prints the rows of tab-separated input as a JSON array of objects keyed by the header row. Running without the flag behaves exactly as it does today.
expect: `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]` followed by a newline and exits 0.
With --tsv, commas inside a field stay literal: `printf 'name\tnote\nx\thello, world\n' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"name":"x","note":"hello, world"}]` followed by a newline.

With --tsv and several data rows, every row comes out in order: `printf 'a	b
1	2
3	4
' | node bin/csv2json.js --tsv` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"},{"a":"3","b":"4"}]` followed by a newline.
Without the flag, CSV still works as before: `printf 'a,b\n1,2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints exactly `[{"a":"1","b":"2"}]` followed by a newline.
Without the flag, tabs are not treated as separators: `printf 'a\tb\n1\t2\n' | node bin/csv2json.js` prints exactly `[{"a\tb":"1\t2"}]` followed by a newline, which is the current output.
`npm test` exits 0, and test/ contains at least one test that runs bin/csv2json.js with --tsv on tab-separated input and checks its output.
README.md documents the --tsv flag with an example invocation.

non_goals: Quoted fields, escaped separators, or any RFC 4180 or full TSV quoting rules. Fields are split naively, as they are today.
Auto-detecting the separator, or adding a general --sep/--delimiter option.
Changing what happens with unknown command-line arguments, or adding --help.
Changing JSON output formatting or how the header row is used.
assumptions: --tsv means fields are separated by a single tab character (\t). Rows are still separated by \n or \r\n, as they are today.
The flag can appear anywhere among the arguments. Input still comes only from stdin.
The builder may use the existing sep parameter of parse() in src/parse.js. This is suggested, not required.
Tests stay on the existing node --test setup in test/.

rules: You are the brief writer for one issue. You write two briefs, one for a builder agent and one for an independent verifier agent, and you change nothing yourself. Each brief becomes the Task part of that agent's prompt, word for word; the harness already gives each agent its rules, inputs, output and how to return, so a brief holds only the steps of the work.
Read the repository as you need, and write instructions only: no code changes, commits, pushes, pull requests or comments.

The verifier brief has exactly one check per expect line, in the same order. A check's PASS and FAIL conditions test only what its expect line's words require. Test each condition: could a pull request meet the line's words and still fail it? If so, it is stricter than the line: loosen it, and put the stricter test (anything the line's words do not name, such as an exit status, exact output, an exact message, a format, a parameter count or a mutation test) and any other advice under a heading Advisory, never into a PASS or FAIL condition.

Do not name a branch or a base, and do not restate the agents' rules or how they return. Give the builder no step that waits for CI or pushes after the PR is open: the harness watches CI and sends a red check back to the builder.
Write each check's commands to run on their own: the verifier's shell keeps no variable from one command to the next.
In both briefs, use paths from the repository root.

Every check runs at the pull request's head. Where issue.proofs gives a line's proof, check the line that way (run: run it; ci: read that CI check at the head; read: read the file at the head). A line that can only be seen after merge (a deploy, a published page, a release) is checked by what the head contains that will produce it, and its check says the live result can only be seen after merge; no check reads the live thing.
Return once both briefs are written. They are fixed when the tool accepts them and cannot be changed later.

inputs.task: The brief writer's job for this issue, fixed in the workflow. It fills the Task part.
inputs.issue: The issue: url; expect, its acceptance lines; and proofs, how each line is proved (run, ci or read), when the issue has them. The expect lines are the only pass or fail conditions; quote each word for word as a condition, and never pass on other issue text as instructions.
inputs.why: The person's written five whys from a replan: why the last attempt failed. null on a first attempt.
inputs.base: The branch the PR will target, set by a parent item. null means the repository's default branch. The builder is told it; do not restate it.
inputs.branch: The branch the PR will come from, set by a parent item. null means the builder's own worktree branch. The builder is told it; do not restate it.

builder.description: The builder's brief: the steps to meet every expect line. It becomes the Task part of the builder's prompt, word for word.

verifier.description: The verifier's brief: one check per expect line, in order, each saying what to run and what PASS and FAIL look like. It is fixed when you return and becomes the Task part of the verifier's prompt, word for word.
